                                              I. INTRODUCTION

          On March 26, 2026, Oncor Electric Delivery Company, LLC ("Oncor") and LCRA
Transmission Services Corporation ("LCRA TSC") (collectively together the "Applicants") filed
a j oint application to amend their Certificates of Convenience and Necessity ("CCN") (the
"Application") for the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV Transmission Line
Proj ect in Bell, Burnet, Concho, Coryell, Lampasas, Llano, Mason, McCulloch, Menard, Milam,

Mills, San Saba, Schleicher, Tom Green, and Williamson Counties (the "Project")·1 The Project
consists of the construction of a new single-circuit 765-kilovolt (kV) transmission line to be built
on steel lattice tower structures, an expansion of Oncor' s existing Bell County East 765/345 kV
switching station, and an expansion of the existing LCRA TSC Big Hill Substation to include a
765/345 kV Station.2 The proposed transmission line is approximately 214 to 244 miles in length,

depending on the route selected by the Commission.3 Depending on the selected route, the
estimated transmission line project cost ranges from approximately $1,636,232,000 to
$1,857,768,000, excluding $395,468,000 in station costs for work at Oncor's Bell County East
Switch.4 Applicants identified Route 894 as the route that best meets the routing criteria in Public
Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) § 37.056 and 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) §

25.101(b)(3)(B).5
         Intervenors M.D. Abel Co. and Joe and Cindy Abel (collectively, the "Abels") own a
family ranch of approximately 1,278 acres located between the cities of Lampasas and Burnet in

Burnet County (the "Property").6 The Property has been in the Abel family for almost 50 years,
has served as the Abels' full-time home since 2002, and supports an active cattle operation that

runs between 50 and 100 head.7 The Abels collectively own the tracts identified in the Application

as Tract Identification Numbers 1861, 1876, 1858, 1863, 1864, 1869, 1872, 1873, and 1874.8 As
established in the Direct Testimony of Cindy Abel, three of the proposed links-Links H2, H3,

interfere with the Abels' home, ranching operation, water resources, and historic structures.'
         Out of the 122 filed alternative routes, only four use any of these links: Route 366 (which

uses Links H3 and H5) and Routes 1241,1242, and 1243 (which use Links H2 and H5).1' Notably,
neither Route 894 nor Route 487 (the route supported by Commission Staff) uses Link H2, H3, or
H5. Not a single intervenor in this proceeding advocated for the use of Links H2, H3, or H5. This
extreme lack of support for Links H2, H3, and H5 reflects the inconsistency of these links with the
PURA routing criteria that the Public Utility Commission ("Commission") must consider. The
Abels strongly oppose Routes 366, 1241, 1242, and 1243, as well as any other route that would
use Link H2, H3, or H5. The Abels, instead, support Route 894 or Route 487, the routes identified

as best meeting the routing criteria set by the Applicants and PUC Staff, respectively.11

                                           II. ROUTING CRITERIA

    A. Including Links H2, H3, or H5 in an approved route would be contrary to the criteria
       that the PUC must consider under PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B).

                i.    Community Values; PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)

         The Commission has previously defined "community values" as: "a shared appreciation of
an area or other natural or human resource by a national, regional, or local community. Adverse
effects upon community values consist of those aspects of a Proposed Project that would
significantly alter the use, enj oyment, or intrinsic value attached to an important area or resource
by a community."12 The Environmental Assessment and Alternative Route Analysis ("EX')
includes a summary of the public comments the Applicants received as part of their public
outreach. Those comments identified shared community values and areas of concern, including

resources, and historic resources.
           The Abels' Property implicates many of these community values, including Residences,
Agriculture and Ranching, Historic Resources, Water Resources, Aesthetics, and Fish and
Wildlife. The Property is the Abels' full-time home and supports an active cattle operation of 50-

100 head. 14 The Property includes the Abels' primary residence and water well, as well as multiple
habitable and historic structures, including the ranch Headquarters-a historic house built in 1890
that serves as the daily operations center for the ranch and in which family and guests regularly
reside-and "Roper's house," a residence constructed in 1915 that the Abels have restored.15 These
homes are of architectural and cultural significance and represent early settlement in this part of
Burnet County.16 The Property also contains the Tumlinson Cemetery, a historic gravesite dating
to 1905; the Property was once owned by T.C. Tumlinson, a Civil War veteran and the first person
                                                                                          17
buried in the cemetery, which is identified on the Applicants' own constraints map.
           Routes using Links H2, H3, or H5 would significantly and adversely impact these
community values. Link H3 would bisect the Property from north to south, passing approximately
600 feet from the Abels' primary residence and approximately 450 feet from their water well, and

would cross South Mesquite Creek, which runs through the Property.18 Link H5 would bisect three
of the Abels' tracts and pass approximately 345 feet from the historic ranch Headquarters, which

the Applicants identified as habitable structure number 499 within 500 feet of Link H5.19 Roper' s

house is located approximately 585 feet from where Link H3 connects with Link H2.2' The
proposed 765-kV transmission line would introduce very large, self-supporting steel lattice
towers-typically 155 to 160 feet tall, with an estimated maximum structure height of 198 feet-

the new right-of-way would fragment the Abels' contiguous ranching operation, disrupt the daily

operations of the ranch, and substantially impair the use and enjoyment of the Abels' home.22
          Route 894 entirely avoids the use of Links H2, H3, and H5, and therefore avoids the Abel
Property. Routes 366, 1241, 1242, and 1243, on the other hand, would impose all of these impacts
on the Abels. The avoidance of habitable structures is itself a shared community value. Route 894
also outperforms the opposed routes on that measure: Route 894 has 85 habitable structures within
500 feet ofits centerline, while Routes 366, 1241, 1242, and 1243 have 131, 144, 135, and 168

habitable structures, respectively-between 45% and 98% more than Route 894.23


               ii.   Aesthetic and Historical Values; PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(C)

          The construction of a 765-kV transmission line on Link H2, H3, or H5 would significantly
diminish the Property' s aesthetic and historical values. The Property is part of the Central Texas
Hill Country and is characterized by gentle rolling hills, native vegetation, and a mix of ranchland

and moderately developed rural areas.24 The proposed line would introduce very large steel lattice
towers visible from nearly all vantage points on the Property and would fundamentally alter the
landscape' s rural character, diminish the Property' s scenic value, interfere with the Abels'
                                                                                                              25
enjoyment of the land, and negatively affect its use as a family ranch and recreational property.
In addition, the Property includes the historic 1890 ranch Headquarters, the 1915 Roper's house,
and the Tumlinson Cemetery, dating to 1905-structures and sites of architectural and cultural

significance that represent early settlement in this part of Burnet County.26 The introduction of a
765-kV transmission line across the Property would detract from this historical character. Route
894 and Route 487 avoid the Property entirely, thereby preserving these aesthetic and historical
values.

                     iii.     Environmental Integrity; PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(D)

 active springs, tanks, surface water bodies, and wildlife.27 South Mesquite Creek runs through the
 Property. Proposed Link H3 would cross directly over South Mesquite Creek, completely ruining
 the Abels' ability to enjoy that creek, and ifLink H5 is part of an approved route, the transmission
 line would be approximately 1,000 feet from the creek and a maj or impediment to its use and
 enjoyment.28

 habitable structures, costs more, crosses more miles of riparian areas and potential wetlands, has

        Links H2, H3, and H5 would introduce very large steel lattice towers across the Property,

requiring a new right-of-way approximately 200 feet wide. 3' Route 366-the only filed route that

uses Link H3-is approximately 14 and 16 miles longer than Route 894 and Route 487,31
respectively, and approximately $100,000,000 more expensive than both Route 894 and Route

487.32 In addition to avoiding additional mileage and costs, Route 894 and 487 would avoid the
environmental impacts on the Property entirely and better protect environmental integrity.


              iv.    Engineering Constraints; 16 TAC § 25.101(c)(3)(B)

        The Applicants' own witness identified runways, airports, and other aviation facilities
                                                                                                                33
among the engineering constraints relevant to routing the Proposed Transmission Line Project.
The portion of the Property along Link H5 is located near a proposed airstrip, which the Applicants
                                                          34
themselves identified on their constraints map.                The introduction of very tall transmission
structures in this area-typically 155 to 160 feet, with a maximum estimated at 198 feet-could
create additional risks and conflicts with aviation operations, which should be avoided where
possible.35 Indeed, the Applicants recognize that when a route is approved using links that cross
                                                                                                                36
or are in proximity to an airstrip, the route may impact or limit the airstrip' s use and operation.
Consistent with these concerns, Routes 1241, 1242, and 1243 each have three private airstrips

within 10,000 feet of the route centerline, compared to two for Route 894.37 Route 894 avoids this
engineering constraint near the Property entirely.

                       v.    Costs; 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)

            The estimated transmission line costs for the Proposed Transmission Line Project range
from approximately $1,636,232,000 to $1,857,768,000, depending on the route selected by the
Commission, excluding approximately $395,468,000 in station costs at Oncor' s Bell County East

Switch.38 Route 894 is the Applicants' identified best-meets route and performs favorably on cost,
with an estimated transmission line cost of $1,680,919,000 and a total estimated proj ect cost of
$2,076,387,000.39
           By contrast, every route that would cross the Abel Property costs more than Route 894.
Route 366 has an estimated transmission line cost of $1,772,384,000-approximately $91,465,000

more than Route 894.*~ Routes 1241, 1242, and 1243 have estimated transmission line costs of
$1,711,580,000,             $1,709,685,000,        and   $1,711,769,000,   respectively-each approximately
$29,000,000 to $31,000,000 more than Route 894.41 Because cost has historically been an
important factor in transmission-line routing decisions, the Commission should give significant
weight to these cost differentials, given the many other advantages Route 894 has over the routes
that would cross the Property.
            The Commission should give significant weight to the fact that either Route 894 or Route

48742 achieves the Applicants' project objectives at a lower cost than any of Routes 366, 1241,
1242, and 1243, while simultaneously avoiding the severe impacts to the Abel Property associated
with Links H2, H3, and H5.


                      vi.   Moderation of Impact on the Affected Community and Landowners; 16
                            TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)

           Minimizing impacts to directly affected landowners is a central consideration under
Commission rules. The record demonstrates that routes containing Link H2, H3, or H5 impose
severe and disproportionate burdens on the Abels.

            As described above, Link H3 would bisect the Property from north to south, passing
approximately 600 feet from the Abels' primary residence and approximately 450 feet from their

water well, and would cross South Mesquite Creek.43 Link H5 would turn west through the
Property and bisect three of the Abels' tracts, passing approximately 345 feet from the historic
                               44
ranch Headquarters.                 The combination of Links H3 and H5 would fragment nearly all of the
Abels' tracts-cutting the ranch from north to south and east to west-and substantially impair the
cattle operation and the Abels' use and enjoyment of their home.45 Link H5 does not follow any
                                                                                          46
existing compatible rights-of-way on the Property and offers no routing benefit.
           By contrast, Route 894 and Route 487 avoid the Property entirely and therefore represent
reasonable and prudent alternatives that significantly moderate landowner impact without
sacrificing proj ect objectives. Broader system benefits do not justify the severe impacts on the
Abels associated with Links H2, H3, and H5, particularly because Routes 366, 1241, 1242, and
1243 do not rank favorably to Routes 894 or 487 on cost, habitable structures, or environmental
impacts. Those routes, therefore, represent precisely the type of disproportionate burden on
individual landowners that the Commission seeks to avoid.

                    vii.      Prudent Avoidance; 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(iv)

           The Commission' s prudent avoidance policy seeks to minimize the public' s exposure to
electric and magnetic fields by avoiding proximity to habitable structures when reasonably
practicable.47 Generally, the Commission evaluates the prudent avoidance policy by seeking to
limit the number of habitable structures within 500 feet of a proposed transmission line, while
considering all routing factors.
           Route 894 performs strongly on prudent avoidance, with 85 habitable structures within 500

feet of its centerline.48 Route 487 only identified 96 habitable structures within 500 feet of its

           In addition to minimizing the number of habitable structures within 500 feet, the
Commission should consider the qualitative nature of those impacts. The Abels' historic ranch
Headquarters-built in 1890, serving as the daily operations center for the ranch, and regularly
housing family and guests-is itself one of the habitable structures (number 499) that the

Commission' s prudent avoidance policy and achieves both prudent avoidance and favorable cost

                III. LINK H42 MEETS PURA CRITERIA FAR BETTER THAN LINK H5

           A route can traverse the area north of the Abel Property from east to west using a single
link-Link H42-without ever entering the Property. The Applicants' own Routes ofInterest Map
confirms this. That map, which the Applicants filed on June 3,2026 and sponsored through their
witness Russell J. Marusak on the first day of the hearing on the merits, was prepared to depict the
routes that the parties substantially discussed and advocated, with a focus on the intervenors' routes
of interest as identified through the parties' Requests for Information.53 As that map illustrates,
Route 894-the route the Applicants identified as best meeting the routing criteria-makes this

east-to-west traverse by way ofLinks Hl, H41, and H42, passing well north ofthe Abel Property.54

         2. Links H3 and H5 Cannot Be Justified as a Substitute for Link Il
        The same problem exists to the south of the Abels' Property. A route can traverse that area
from east to west using a single link-Link Il-running from Link G-6 to Link J3 1 without crossing
the Property. The Applicants' Routes of Interest Map again confirms that Link Il is the single-link
path through this area, and, as Mr. Marusak explained on the first day of the hearing, that map was
assembled to show the routes the parties actually contested, focused on the intervenors' routes of
                                                          57
interest drawn from the Requests for Information.
        To make this same east-to-west connection without Link Il, a route must substitute two
links that cross the Abel Property: Link H3 and Link H5. Route 366-the only filed route that uses
                                                                                                58
Link H3-does exactly that, running G6-H3-H5-J31 in place of G6-Il-J31.                               The correct
comparison is therefore between the single Link Il and the combination of Links H3 and H5 that
replaces it. Here too, the substitution is the worse choice. As the table below shows, the H3-plus-
H5 detour is nearly four miles longer than Link Il, places more habitable structures within 500
feet of the line (nine versus eight), more than doubles the number of stream crossings (twenty
versus eight), and adds electronic installations and additional recorded cultural resources,
including a recorded cultural-resource site crossed by the line. The only measure on which the H3-
plus-H5 detour is lower is riparian-area mileage. That single point does not justify the additional
length, the additional habitable-structure and stream-crossing impacts, or the severe, Property-
specific harms that Links H3 and H5 inflict on the Abels.
